analysis.one_liner: Restores broad disability discrimination protections that Supreme Court rulings had narrowed.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee held one hearing but never voted; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: After a string of Supreme Court decisions, workers with conditions like diabetes, epilepsy, or cancer that are controlled by medication were being ruled out of Americans with Disabilities Act protection as not 'disabled enough.' This bill would have rewritten the ADA's definition of disability to cover anyone facing adverse treatment because of an actual or perceived impairment, told courts to ignore whether a person uses medication or assistive devices when deciding coverage, and required the law to be read broadly. It never advanced beyond a committee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants with physical or mental impairments — including people whose conditions are managed with medication, glasses, or assistive devices — who lost ADA protection after the Supreme Court's Sutton and Toyota decisions. The bill would have let them sue for discrimination based on an actual or perceived impairment, made adverse action over the use of a mitigating measure (like insulin) itself discrimination, and required courts and agencies to defer to regulations implementing the broader standard [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes 'substantially limits a major life activity' from the definition of disability, so a person need not prove their impairment severely limits them to be covered [S2] [S3].

Bars employers from arguing that medication, prosthetics, or other mitigating measures make an impairment less disabling, and makes firing or penalizing someone for using such a measure an act of discrimination [S2] [S3].
Covers people with impairments that are episodic, in remission, or latent (for example, cancer in remission or epilepsy with controlled seizures) [S3].
Protects people perceived as having an impairment even if they do not, and people with a record of misclassification as impaired [S3].

Requires the Act to be broadly construed and directs the Attorney General, EEOC, and Transportation Secretary to write implementing regulations within 180 days, with courts required to defer to that guidance [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — private businesses, governments, and other covered entities — would bear more disability discrimination claims, broader accommodation obligations, and the cost of complying with new regulations and accessibility guidelines issued after enactment [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill covers far more people than the post-2002 case law did, and employers argued this would sweep in impairments with little workplace effect and increase litigation and accommodation costs, a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge since the bill itself keeps no filter beyond the 'qualified individual' defense [S3].

It still requires a plaintiff to be a 'qualified individual with a disability' as an employer defense, but by replacing the old 'because of the disability' standard with discrimination 'on the basis of disability,' it makes nearly any adverse action tied to an impairment potentially actionable, shifting significant legal risk onto covered employers [S3].

The bill directs agencies and courts to give deference to its regulations and guidance, which reduces the ability of courts to narrow the protections later — a feature supporters wanted and opponents viewed as tying courts' hands [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial and well-documented in the bill's own findings: Supreme Court decisions had eliminated ADA protection for people Congress originally meant to cover, such as workers whose diabetes or epilepsy is controlled by medication [S3]. The cost is real — a much larger universe of covered claims and higher compliance and litigation exposure for employers — but the bill preserves the employer's defense that a plaintiff is not a qualified individual, so it shifts the boundary rather than removing it entirely [S3]. The tradeoff favors workers with impairments and disadvantages employers, particularly those with marginal accommodation claims.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate committee that handles labor and disability law, and got one hearing in November 2007 — but the committee never marked it up and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on July 26, 2007, joined by Sen. Arlen Specter, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S3] [S5].
Three senators (2 Republicans and 1 Democrat) cosponsored the bill [S4].
The HELP Committee held a hearing on the bill on November 15, 2007, with the hearing printed as S.Hrg. 110-773 [S5].
No further action was taken — no committee vote, no Senate floor vote — and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers benefited from the bill's death: the narrowed Supreme Court standard remained in force, so businesses kept the ability to defeat disability claims on the ground that a plaintiff's impairment, once mitigated by medication or devices, no longer 'substantially limited' a major life activity. Workers with controlled impairments remained outside the ADA's protection.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the ADA Restoration Act and spoke for it at introduction; the Senate referred it to the HELP Committee, where a hearing was held.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Joined Harkin in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the broadest version of the ADA restoration and pressed for a narrower, negotiated definition of disability, with which the broader bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican, with cosponsorship split 2 Republicans to 1 Democrat; no votes were ever taken, so party positions on passage were never recorded.

industries.industry: Employers (private businesses and other covered entities)
industries.note: The bill would have expanded the pool of workers who can bring disability discrimination claims and barred defenses based on mitigating measures like medication, raising litigation and accommodation costs for employers. Their interest in keeping the post-Sutton narrower standard ran against workers with controlled impairments.
The advocates' client base — workers with impairments — lost the chance at restored protection when the bill died; their interest ran alongside ordinary workers' interests.
